title: Annotate a commit without rewriting it
summary: git notes attach text to a commit after the fact — review outcomes, CI results, incident links — without changing its sha. Learn why they are invisible by default, and how to share them.
concepts: notes do not change the sha
mental_model: A commit is immutable, so anything learned after it was made cannot go in its message. Notes live in a separate ref and are attached by sha — mutable metadata bolted onto immutable history.

steps.title: The problem notes solve
steps.why: Six weeks after a commit shipped, you learn it caused an incident. That fact belongs with the commit — but amending it would rewrite history everyone has pulled, for a comment.
commands: sh -c 'echo pump commit: $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump")'
steps.expect: Three commits, one of which needs annotating.

steps.title: Attach a note
steps.why: `notes add` writes the text into a separate ref keyed by commit sha. The commit object is untouched, so nothing downstream of it changes.

actions.run: sh -c 'git notes add -m "Caused INC-2026-014: pump cavitation above 1500 RPM. Reverted in production, re-landed with a ramp in the next release." $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump")'

commands: sh -c 'git notes show $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump")'
steps.expect: The note prints, and the log looks exactly as before.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'git notes show $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump")'
verify.label: the note is attached to the commit

steps.title: Prove the sha did not change
steps.why: This is the entire point. Compare the commit's sha before and after — identical — which is why notes are safe to add to public history and amending is not.
steps.expect: A commit object with no note in it — the note lives elsewhere.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'git cat-file -p $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump") | grep -c INC-2026 || true'
verify.label: the commit object itself is unchanged

steps.title: Find where notes actually live
steps.why: `refs/notes/commits` is an ordinary ref pointing at an ordinary commit, whose tree maps commit shas to note blobs. Nothing exotic — which means every recovery trick you know still applies.
steps.expect: A notes ref, its own commit history, and a tree keyed by commit sha.

steps.title: See them in the log
steps.why: `git log` shows notes by default in most versions; `--notes` forces it and `--no-notes` hides them. In a format string, `%N` prints the note — useful for building an annotated changelog.
steps.expect: The note attached under its commit, and absent when suppressed.

steps.title: Use a namespace for machine-written notes
steps.why: `--ref` gives notes their own namespace, so CI results do not collide with human annotations. This is how build systems record test outcomes and durations against a commit.

actions.run: sh -c 'git notes --ref=ci add -m "build=passed duration=94s runner=linux-x64" $(git log -1 --format=%H)'
sh -c 'git notes --ref=ci add -m "build=failed duration=31s runner=linux-x64" $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump")'

verify.label: CI results live in their own notes namespace

steps.title: Notes are not pushed by default
steps.why: This is why most people have never seen one. `git push` sends branches and, with `--follow-tags`, tags — never notes. They need their refspec naming explicitly.
steps.expect: Zero notes refs on the server after a normal push, both of them after the explicit one.

verify.label: notes reached the server once pushed explicitly

steps.title: Make fetching them automatic
steps.why: Adding a fetch refspec means colleagues receive notes with an ordinary `git fetch`. Without this, a note you push is invisible to everyone — the single reason notes are rare in practice.

verify.label: notes are fetched alongside branches from now on

steps.title: Edit and remove
steps.why: Notes are mutable — that is their advantage and their weakness. Editing one leaves no trace in the commit, and two people editing the same note conflict like any other ref.
commands: sh -c 'git notes append -m "Prevention: added a ramp and a regression test." $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump")'
sh -c 'git notes show $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump")'

verify.cmd: sh -c 'git notes show $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump")'
verify.label: the note was extended without touching the commit

verify.cmd: sh -c 'git notes show $(git log -1 --format=%H --grep="Raise the pump")'
verify.label: the incident annotation is attached to the commit that caused it
verify.hint: git notes add, then git notes append

verify.label: history is unchanged — notes never rewrite anything
the notes were published to the server
verify.hint: they need their own refspec; a normal push ignores them

verify.label: colleagues will now receive notes on an ordinary fetch

pitfalls: Notes are invisible by default because they are neither pushed nor fetched without an explicit refspec. Configure both, or nobody else will ever see them.
A rebase or amend changes the commit sha, and the note stays attached to the OLD sha. `notes.rewriteRef` can carry them across rewrites, but it is off for rebase by default.
Two people editing the same note produce a conflict on `refs/notes/commits`, resolved with `git notes merge`. It is rarer and stranger than a normal merge conflict.
Because notes are mutable and unsigned, they are metadata, not evidence. Anything that must be tamper-evident belongs in the commit message.
Forges vary in support: some display notes, some ignore them entirely. Do not build a process on them without checking.
cheatsheet: attach a note to a commit
a separate namespace for machine data
